guides.title: Cold & Hypothermia
guides.summary: Layering, frostbite, hypothermia and staying warm.

sections.heading: Spot hypothermia
sections.body:
Hypothermia is a fall in core body temperature below about 35 °C (95 °F), and the reason it kills people who could have been saved is that its earliest sign is a loss of the judgement needed to recognise it. The field mnemonic is the umbles: stumbles, mumbles, fumbles and grumbles. Coordination degrades first — a person trips on ground they walked over an hour ago, drops a zip pull, cannot work a buckle. Speech slurs or becomes clipped. Reasoning narrows and mood turns flat or irritable. If someone in the cold cannot pass a simple test such as walking a straight line heel-to-toe for ten paces, treat that as hypothermia and act, regardless of what they insist about feeling fine.

Field staging matters because it changes the treatment. In mild hypothermia (roughly 35–32 °C / 95–90 °F) the person is conscious and shivering hard; shivering is still generating heat, and this stage is reversible with insulation, shelter and calories. In moderate hypothermia (roughly 32–28 °C / 90–82 °F) shivering weakens or stops altogether and consciousness is visibly impaired — that transition, not any thermometer, is the practical dividing line, and it signals a person who can no longer rewarm themselves. Below about 28 °C the person is usually unconscious with a slow, faint pulse and may appear dead.

Treatment for a mild case is straightforward: get out of the wind, remove every wet layer, wrap the person in dry insulation including a barrier underneath them against the ground, add a vapour barrier such as a bivvy bag or plastic sheet, and give warm sweet drinks — but only to someone fully alert enough to hold and swallow safely. Sugar matters because shivering is burning glucose fast. Gentle movement helps a mild case; strenuous exertion does not.

Once shivering has stopped, the handling rules change sharply and are the part most often got wrong. Move the person as little and as gently as possible and keep them horizontal. Cold, stiff heart muscle is electrically unstable, and rough handling or standing a moderately hypothermic person up can trigger a fatal arrhythmia — the phenomenon behind deaths that occur after rescue rather than before it. Do not put a moderate or severe case in a hot bath or shower; peripheral vasodilation dumps cold, acidic blood back to the heart. Apply heat packs wrapped in cloth to the chest, armpits and back rather than to the limbs, insulate thoroughly, and evacuate.

Two further points. Alcohol worsens hypothermia by dilating skin vessels — the warm flush is core heat leaving. And in a suspected hypothermic cardiac arrest, check for a pulse for a full 60 seconds before concluding there is none, because a profoundly slowed heart is easy to miss.

sections.heading: Frostbite
sections.body:
Frostbite is the actual freezing of tissue, and it damages in two stages. Ice crystals form first in the fluid between cells and then, as freezing deepens, inside the cells themselves, rupturing membranes. The second and often larger injury arrives on rewarming, when blood returns to vessels whose linings were damaged by the freeze: clots form in the smallest vessels, inflammatory chemicals flood the area, and tissue that survived the freeze dies from lack of blood supply. This is why the depth of injury frequently cannot be judged for days, and why any confident early prediction of tissue loss should be distrusted.

Frostnip is the reversible precursor — skin blanches white or waxy, feels numb and prickly, but stays soft to the touch. Rewarm it immediately by skin-to-skin contact, tucking fingers into an armpit or against the belly, or cupping a bare warm hand over a nipped ear or nose. There is no lasting damage if it is caught here. Frostbite proper feels hard, wooden or rubbery, and the numbness is complete rather than tingling.

Rewarming is done in circulating water held at 37–39 °C (99–102 °F) — measured with a thermometer if at all possible, or judged by a helper's uninjured elbow finding it comfortably warm and never hot — for 15 to 30 minutes, until the tissue turns red or purple and becomes pliable. Hotter water burns tissue that cannot feel it. Never use dry heat: a fire, a stove, a vehicle exhaust or a heater will cause deep burns in numb flesh, and this accounts for a large share of the worst outcomes. Never rub or massage frozen tissue; ice crystals shear cells apart mechanically.

The single most important field decision is whether refreezing is possible. Tissue that thaws and refreezes is injured far more severely than tissue that stays frozen, so if the casualty must still walk out through cold, or shelter and heat cannot be guaranteed, leave the part frozen, pad and splint it, and evacuate. Walking on frozen feet is survivable; walking on thawed ones is not.

Rewarming is intensely painful, and strong analgesia should be available before starting. Ibuprofen is commonly recommended both for pain and because it blocks some of the inflammatory pathway driving reperfusion injury; typical wilderness guidance is 400 mg every 8 to 12 hours in an adult with no contraindication. Afterwards, separate the affected digits with dry gauze, cover loosely, elevate to limit swelling, and do not allow the person to walk on a thawed foot. Leave blisters intact. Blood-filled blisters indicate deeper injury than clear ones. All true frostbite warrants medical assessment, and severe cases treated within about 24 hours may be candidates for clot-dissolving drugs that can save digits.

sections.heading: Layer for cold
sections.body:
A layering system works because the insulation is not the fabric but the still air trapped inside and between the layers. Anything that displaces that air — compression, water, or wind driving through it — destroys the insulation regardless of how thick the garment looks. Three functional layers do the work: a wicking base against the skin, an insulating mid layer that holds air, and a wind- and waterproof shell that stops moving air stripping the warmth away.

The base layer's job is to move sweat off the skin, not to keep you warm. Merino wool in the 150–250 g/m² range and synthetic polyester knits both do this; the practical difference is that wool resists odour and retains a useful fraction of its insulation when damp, while synthetics dry faster and cost less. Cotton is the one material to exclude entirely. It absorbs many times its own weight in water, holds it against the skin, collapses its air spaces and then cools you by evaporation — the origin of the blunt maxim that cotton kills. A cotton T-shirt under a good jacket can undo the whole system.

The mid layer supplies the trapped air. Fleece is bulky but keeps insulating when damp and dries quickly. Down offers the best warmth for its weight, with fill power from roughly 600 to 900 measuring how much loft an ounce provides, but wet down clumps and loses almost all of its value, so it belongs in dry cold or under a reliable shell. Synthetic fill is heavier and less compressible but keeps a large share of its insulation when wet, which makes it the safer choice in damp maritime cold.

The shell stops convection. A windproof layer alone can be worth several degrees, because wind removes the warmed boundary layer of air against you; waterproof-breathable membranes add rain protection at the cost of some vapour transfer.

The system is only as good as its regulation, and the discipline is to start out feeling slightly cold. Sweat is the enemy: once a base layer is soaked, it will chill you hard the moment you stop, and it may not dry before nightfall. Vent early — open pit zips, remove a hat, drop the shell — rather than waiting until you are damp.

Extremities and head need deliberate attention. Uncovered skin loses heat directly, and a hat plus a neck gaiter closes the largest easily-sealed gaps. Boots must be sized to fit a thick sock without pressure, because a tight boot compresses insulation and restricts circulation, and cold feet in tight boots are usually a fit problem rather than a warmth problem. Mittens beat gloves for warmth because fingers share air space. In extreme, prolonged cold a vapour-barrier liner sock or shirt prevents sweat saturating insulation over multi-day trips.

sections.heading: Stay warm
sections.body:
Staying warm over hours and days is a matter of managing four things continuously: wind, moisture, fuel and contact with cold surfaces. None of them is dramatic, and that is precisely why people get caught out — the failures accumulate quietly.

Wind is the first and largest lever, because moving air strips away the thin envelope of warmed air your body maintains against the skin and forces you to reheat a fresh layer continuously. Getting behind a ridge, a wall, a vehicle, a snow bank or a stand of dense trees can be worth more than any single garment. When there is nothing to shelter behind, build something: a low wall of snow blocks, packs, or piled brush on the windward side changes the situation immediately. Facing away from the wind and sitting rather than standing both help, since wind speed rises with height above the ground.

Moisture is the second. Wet insulation is not insulation, and the water usually comes from you rather than from the sky. Vent before you sweat, not after — the moment you notice you are working hard, open a zip or shed a layer, because a base layer that becomes soaked during an hour of effort will chill you severely during the twenty-minute stop that follows. Dry socks before sleeping are close to non-negotiable; damp socks in a sleeping bag will keep feet cold all night and can set up trench foot over successive days. Damp gloves and hats can be dried overnight against the body inside a sleeping bag.

Fuel matters because your heat is metabolic. Eating and drinking regularly is not comfort but function: shivering can multiply heat production several times over, and it burns through blood glucose quickly. Thirst is unreliable in cold air, so drink on a schedule rather than on sensation. Alcohol is actively harmful — the flush of warmth it produces is core heat being dumped through dilated skin vessels, and it also blunts the judgement needed to notice trouble.

Contact with cold surfaces drains heat faster than air does, because solids and liquids conduct far better than still air. Never sit directly on snow, rock or metal; put a pack, a foam pad, a coil of rope or even a stack of branches underneath you. A sleeping pad is more important than a warmer sleeping bag, because bag insulation crushed under body weight has almost no value.

Finally, keep temperature-sensitive equipment inside your clothing. Lithium and alkaline cells lose a substantial fraction of their usable capacity near and below freezing, and a butane lighter may not vaporise fuel at all when cold. Spare batteries, a lighter, a phone and any medication belong in an inner pocket against the torso, not in a pack lid.

sections.heading: How Your Body Loses Heat: The Physics of Cold Exposure
sections.body:
Core body temperature is defended within roughly half a degree of 37 °C (98.6 °F), and every technique in cold-weather practice is an attempt to slow one or more of five physical heat-loss pathways: radiation, conduction, convection, evaporation and respiration. Knowing which pathway dominates in a given situation is what turns a list of tips into a decision.

Radiation is heat leaving the body as infrared energy, and it needs no contact or air movement at all. At rest in still, moderate air it accounts for the largest single share of loss, and it flows from any uncovered skin toward whatever is colder — which on a clear night includes the open sky, effectively at a radiative temperature far below the air. This is why covering the head and neck buys more than their modest surface area suggests, and why a shelter with a roof feels warmer than an open windbreak even when the air temperature is identical.

Conduction is direct transfer into whatever you touch. Its magnitude depends on the material: still air conducts heat at roughly 0.024 watts per metre-kelvin, while water conducts at about 0.6 — some twenty-five times faster. That single ratio explains why wet clothing is dangerous rather than merely unpleasant, why sitting on frozen ground drains you, and why immersion in cold water is an emergency on a completely different timescale from standing in cold air.

Convection is heat carried off by moving air or water, and it is what wind chill measures. Your body warms a thin boundary layer of air against the skin; wind removes it continuously so that the reheating never finishes. Convective loss rises steeply with wind speed at low speeds and then flattens, which is why the first few miles per hour of wind matter far more than the difference between strong and very strong wind.

Evaporation cools you whenever moisture leaves skin or lungs, at roughly 2,400 kilojoules per litre of water evaporated. The same mechanism that saves you in summer works against you in winter: sweat produced during exertion continues evaporating after you stop, and it is drawing that heat out of you. Respiration combines the last two, losing both heat and water with every exhaled breath, which is one reason fluid and calorie needs climb in cold, dry air.

Shivering is the emergency response — involuntary, asynchronous muscle contraction that can raise metabolic heat production roughly two to five times above resting levels. It is genuinely effective in the short term and genuinely unsustainable, because it consumes glucose rapidly and fatigues. Shivering is a signal to add insulation, get out of the wind, eat, or start moving. It is never a plan.

sections.heading: Reading Wind Chill: Why the Thermometer Lies to You
sections.body:
Air temperature alone says very little about how fast exposed skin will cool, because moving air continuously removes the warmed boundary layer against the skin. The United States National Weather Service and Environment Canada adopted a shared wind chill standard in 2001 based on a model of heat loss from an exposed adult face at walking pace, and the North American formula in Fahrenheit and miles per hour is WCT = 35.74 + 0.6215T − 35.75·V^0.16 + 0.4275·T·V^0.16. The metric version, in degrees Celsius and kilometres per hour, is 13.12 + 0.6215T − 11.37·V^0.16 + 0.3965·T·V^0.16.

The numbers are worth working once, because intuition underestimates them. At an air temperature of 20 °F with a 20 mph wind, V^0.16 is about 1.615, so the equation gives 35.74 + 12.43 − 57.74 + 13.81, which is about 4 °F — a sixteen-degree effective drop. At 5 °F with a 25 mph wind, the same arithmetic yields roughly −17 °F. The relationship is strongly non-linear in wind speed: because the wind term carries an exponent of 0.16, going from calm to 5 mph costs far more than going from 30 mph to 35 mph.

The practical output is exposure time. On the standard chart, frostbite of exposed facial skin becomes likely within about 30 minutes near a wind chill of −18 °F (−28 °C), within about 10 minutes near −33 °F (−36 °C), and within roughly 5 minutes near −48 °F (−44 °C). Those thresholds assume bare skin; a face covered by a balaclava is not on the chart at all.

Two misunderstandings are common and both matter. First, wind chill is a skin-exposure index, not a physical temperature. An object cannot be cooled below the actual air temperature by wind — a water bottle, a car engine or a pipe will approach the true air temperature faster in wind, but never go below it. Announcements that pipes will freeze because the wind chill is −20 when the air is 20 °F are simply wrong. Second, the model assumes the person is walking at about 3 mph, so it already includes a small self-generated component; conversely, cycling, skiing or riding in an open vehicle on a calm day creates a real wind chill that no weather forecast will mention.

The honest limitation is that the index models a healthy adult face and ignores humidity, sunshine and clothing. Direct sun can offset several degrees; damp air and inadequate cover make the real risk worse than the number implies. Treat the chart as a planning tool for exposure limits, not a precise prediction. Children, the elderly, anyone with impaired circulation and anyone already wet or dehydrated will be affected sooner than the chart suggests, and none of that appears in the equation.

sections.heading: Cold-Water Immersion and the 1-10-1 Rule
sections.body:
Falling into cold water is a faster and structurally different emergency from dry cold exposure, and it kills in a predictable sequence captured by the 1-10-1 rule popularised by the cold-physiology researcher Gordon Giesbrecht. The single most useful thing about the rule is that it corrects the near-universal assumption that hypothermia is what kills you. It usually is not.

The first 1 is one minute of cold shock. Sudden skin cooling triggers an involuntary gasp of one to three litres, followed by uncontrollable hyperventilation lasting a minute or more, along with a sharp rise in heart rate and blood pressure. If the gasp happens underwater, the person drowns immediately; if the hyperventilation continues, they cannot hold a breath or coordinate a swim stroke. The response peaks in water around 10–15 °C and is largely over within about a minute. The entire strategy for this phase is to keep the airway clear, hold on to something, and wait for the breathing to settle before attempting anything else. Panicking through it is what drowns people.

The 10 is roughly ten minutes of meaningful movement. Cold rapidly cools the nerves and muscles of the arms and hands, and grip strength and fine control fall away long before core temperature has moved at all. This is the entire self-rescue window: get out, get onto something floating, get a flotation device secured, or reach a fixed object and hold on while you still can. Most cold-water drownings are swim failures inside this window rather than hypothermia deaths.

The final 1 is around one hour before hypothermia causes unconsciousness — longer in warmer water, with more body fat, or with better insulation, and shorter for a thin person in near-freezing water. The practical consequence is optimistic and often surprising: someone floating in cold water usually has far more survivable time than they believe, provided they stop struggling and conserve heat.

If escape is impossible, adopt the Heat Escape Lessening Posture: knees drawn to the chest, arms clamped across the chest, wearing a flotation device that keeps the head clear without effort. This protects the sides of the chest, the armpits and the groin, where large vessels run close to the surface. In a group, huddle chest to chest with children or thin people in the middle. Keep clothing on — the layer of water trapped inside warms slightly and still insulates, and removing clothes in water gains nothing and costs energy. Get as much of the body out of the water as possible onto any floating object, since air, even cold air, conducts heat far more slowly than water. Treat every rescued immersion victim gently and horizontally, since a body chilled in water is as vulnerable to rough handling as any other hypothermia casualty, and remove wet clothing only once wind protection and dry insulation are actually ready to replace it.

sections.heading: Non-Freezing Cold Injuries: Trench Foot and Chilblains
sections.body:
Tissue does not have to freeze to be seriously damaged, and the non-freezing cold injuries are the ones most likely to end an otherwise well-equipped trip. They occur in the temperature band people treat as merely uncomfortable, which is exactly why they get ignored until the damage is done.

Trench foot, also called immersion foot, develops when feet are kept wet and cold — typically between about 0 and 15 °C (32–59 °F) — for a prolonged period without ever freezing. Sustained cold and damp keep the small blood vessels constricted; the tissue is starved of oxygen for hours on end, and both the vessel walls and the small nerves are progressively damaged. Onset can be as short as ten to fourteen hours in wet, cold, immobile conditions, though one to three days is more typical. Early signs are numbness and a heavy, wooden feeling, with skin that is blotchy white, red or blue, cold to touch, and often swollen. In advanced cases blisters form and tissue dies. The name comes from the static, waterlogged trenches of the First World War, where it caused tens of thousands of casualties, but it takes nothing more exotic than boots that leak and no chance to dry out.

Prevention is almost entirely moisture management and it is genuinely effective. Change out of wet socks as soon as practical, dry the feet thoroughly at every rest break — even ten minutes with boots and socks off in still air makes a difference — carry at least two spare pairs so a dry pair always exists, and dry damp socks overnight against the body. Keeping the feet moving to maintain circulation matters too, which is part of why the injury was so severe among troops who stood still for days.

Chilblains, medically called pernio, are a distinct and usually milder injury from repeated exposure to cold, damp air rather than immersion. Small itchy or painful red-to-purple bumps appear on fingers, toes, ears and the nose, generally twelve to twenty-four hours after exposure and resolving over one to three weeks. The leading explanation is that vessels constricted by cold respond abnormally to rewarming, allowing fluid to leak from capillaries into the surrounding tissue and producing localised inflammation.

Both conditions are treated the same cautious way, and the rules are the opposite of intuition. Rewarm gradually at ordinary room temperature. Do not use hot water, a fire, a heater or a hot water bottle, because numbed tissue cannot report a burn until it is done. Do not rub or massage the area. Elevate to reduce swelling, keep the skin scrupulously dry afterwards, dress any blistering or broken skin as a wound and watch for infection, and expect residual cold sensitivity in the affected part for months or years.

sections.heading: Fueling the Furnace: Nutrition and Hydration in the Cold
sections.body:
Cold exposure is metabolically expensive, and underfeeding is one of the quieter ways a well-equipped person becomes a casualty. Shivering alone can raise energy expenditure two to five times above resting, and it is layered on top of the ordinary costs of moving through snow, breaking trail and carrying several extra kilograms of clothing. Sustained cold-weather activity commonly pushes daily requirements into the range of 4,000 to 6,000 kilocalories, roughly double a temperate-climate day, and polar expedition rations are built around figures at the top of that band or beyond.

Composition matters as much as quantity. Fat supplies about 9 kilocalories per gram against roughly 4 for carbohydrate and protein, and it digests slowly, which makes high-fat foods — nuts, cheese, butter, fatty cured meats, chocolate — disproportionately valuable for sustained output and for the long overnight period. Carbohydrate is the fuel shivering actually burns and is depleted fastest, so simple carbohydrate is best reserved for immediate use before or during effort. A practical pattern is a fat-heavy meal before sleep, since digestion itself generates heat through the night, and frequent small carbohydrate snacks during the day rather than two large stops. Protein does not warm you efficiently and, eaten alone in quantity, increases water demand.

Hydration is the half most often neglected, because thirst is an unreliable signal in the cold. Cold-induced diuresis is the mechanism: peripheral vessels constrict, blood is shunted toward the core, the kidneys read the resulting central volume as excess and shed fluid through increased urination. Simultaneously, every breath exhaled into cold, dry air carries away water — the visible cloud is real loss. The result is that people dehydrate steadily in winter without ever feeling thirsty, and dehydration then reduces blood volume available to carry heat to the extremities, so cold tolerance worsens and frostbite risk rises.

The fix is scheduled drinking rather than drinking on sensation — a defined amount every hour, tracked deliberately. Warm drinks are easier to consume in quantity and their warmth is psychologically useful, though the heat they add is small compared with the calories in them. Eating snow is a bad exchange: melting it inside you costs roughly 334 kilojoules per kilogram of ice at the melting point alone, before any warming, and it chills the mouth and core. Melt snow over a stove instead and budget fuel accordingly, since melting and heating water is often the largest single fuel expense of a winter camp.

Alcohol deserves a specific warning. It causes peripheral vasodilation, producing a convincing sensation of warmth that is in fact accelerated core heat loss, and it impairs both shivering and the judgement needed to recognise trouble. The traditional brandy given to a cold casualty is one of the more durable pieces of dangerous folklore, and caffeine, while far less harmful, is a mild diuretic that adds nothing useful to a fluid budget already under strain.

sections.heading: Building Emergency Shelter and Fire in Snow
sections.body:
Snow is an excellent insulator, which surprises people until they remember that it is mostly trapped air. Undisturbed low-density snow has a thermal conductivity around 0.05 to 0.15 watts per metre-kelvin — closer to fleece than to ice — and a shelter dug into it can hold an interior near 0 °C (32 °F) while the outside air sits at −25 °C, purely by blocking wind and cutting off radiant loss to the night sky. The insulation is not free warmth; it is the elimination of the two fastest loss pathways plus whatever heat your body and a candle contribute.

Two designs cover most situations. A snow cave is dug into a deep, firm drift or a bank, which requires a drift at least about two metres deep. A quinzhee is built where no drift exists: shovel loose snow into a mound roughly two to two and a half metres across and a metre and a half high, then leave it undisturbed for at least one to two hours so the disturbed crystals sinter and bond into a self-supporting mass, then hollow it out. Skipping the settling period is the usual reason a quinzhee collapses. Pushing thirty-centimetre sticks into the mound before hollowing gives a wall-thickness gauge from inside — when digging exposes a stick tip, stop.

The single most important interior detail is a raised sleeping platform above the entrance level. Cold air is denser and sinks, so a shelter with a low trench near the door and a shelf above it drains the coldest air away from the occupant continuously. A doorway plugged loosely with a pack completes the arrangement. Ventilation is not optional: punch a fist-sized hole through the roof with a ski pole or stick and check periodically that it has not glazed over. In a sealed snow shelter, carbon dioxide accumulates, and if any stove or flame is used inside, carbon monoxide can reach lethal levels without warning. Dig with the shell on and the insulation off, because building one is hard, sweaty work and soaking your layers defeats the purpose.

Fire in snow requires bringing your own reliable tinder rather than hoping to find dry material. Petroleum-jelly-soaked cotton balls, dryer lint, birch bark or commercial fire cubes in a waterproof container all work; a ferrocerium rod throws sparks of around 3,000 °C and functions when wet, unlike a butane lighter, whose fuel may not vaporise below about −5 °C unless warmed against the body.

For on-site fuel, take dead branches still attached to standing trees rather than anything lying on wet ground, and shave feather sticks to expose dry inner wood. Build on a platform of green logs or thick bark laid over the snow — without one, the fire melts its own pit, sinks into meltwater and drowns itself.

sections.heading: Getting the Gear
sections.body:
Technique cannot compensate for equipment that fails, and cold-weather gear fails in specific, predictable ways worth understanding before spending money on it.

Boots and sleeping systems deserve the largest share of the budget because they address conduction, the fastest loss path outside water. A removable liner is not a luxury: liners absorb foot sweat, and a liner that can be pulled out and dried inside a sleeping bag overnight is the difference between starting the second day warm and starting it in damp insulation. Boot sizing is the most common and most damaging error — a boot bought to fit snugly then worn with a thick sock compresses the insulation and restricts blood flow, and cold feet from this cause cannot be fixed by any amount of extra sock.

Sleeping bag ratings need reading with scepticism. The EN and ISO standards report a comfort rating, aimed at a standard adult woman sleeping relaxed, and a lower rating for a standard adult man sleeping curled; marketing usually quotes the lower number. Choosing a bag rated well below the coldest expected night builds in margin for an optimistic rating, lost loft with age, and a night colder than forecast. Underneath it, a closed-cell foam pad is the component people skip and should not, because bag insulation compressed by body weight has almost no value. Foam keeps working when punctured; an inflatable pad adds warmth but can fail.

Stoves are the other predictable failure. Ordinary butane and isobutane canisters lose vapour pressure as they cool and may not run at all near and below freezing; liquid-fuel stoves burning white gas are pressurised by pumping and are largely indifferent to temperature, which is why they remain standard for serious winter use. Insulated wide-mouth bottles matter because a narrow cap freezes shut and a wide mouth can be cleared of ice, and storing a bottle upside down in snow keeps the ice from forming at the cap. Chemical warmers need air to work and will not activate inside an airtight bag.
ingredients: Insulated, waterproof boots with removable liners, sized to allow a thick sock without cutting off circulation, from an outdoor/camping retailer
Wool or synthetic base-layer thermal underwear (top and bottom) — avoid cotton, which loses nearly all insulating value when wet
A sleeping bag rated at least 10-15°F below the coldest temperature you expect to encounter, from an outdoor/camping retailer
A closed-cell foam sleeping pad, ideally paired with an inflatable pad, for insulation from the cold ground
Chemical hand and toe warmers (air-activated iron-oxide packets), sold individually or by the box at any outdoor or hardware store
A stove rated for cold weather — standard butane/isobutane canister stoves lose pressure below freezing; a white-gas or cold-weather-blend canister stove performs more reliably
A wind- and waterproof hard-shell outer jacket and pants
A wide-mouth, insulated water bottle or vacuum flask (a narrow-mouth bottle's cap can freeze shut)
A fire-starting kit: waterproof or strike-anywhere matches, or a ferrocerium rod, plus manufactured tinder such as petroleum-jelly cotton balls
A basic first-aid kit with supplies suited to blisters and skin injuries, from a pharmacy
A compact outdoor thermometer to track actual ambient temperature rather than guessing
An avalanche beacon, collapsible shovel, and probe if traveling in snow-covered mountain terrain, from a mountaineering/outdoor retailer

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Running a Cold-Weather Readiness Drill
sections.body:
Gear that has never been tested is an assumption, not a plan, and the assumption usually fails at the worst moment. A readiness drill is a deliberately low-stakes rehearsal run close to shelter, and its purpose is to convert vague confidence into specific knowledge: which of your fingers goes numb first, how many minutes of walking before your base layer is damp, whether you can actually work your zips wearing the gloves you own.

Run it somewhere you can be warm and indoors within a few minutes, and treat any numbness beyond mild tingling as the signal to stop immediately rather than a challenge to endure. Build up incrementally — a calm day before a windy one, a short session before a long one — because both cold tolerance and honest self-assessment develop with exposure. Write the findings down afterwards while they are fresh; the item you failed to reach for is as informative as the one you used constantly.
steps: Choose a genuinely cold, dry day (air temperature at or below 32°F/0°C) and run this drill somewhere you can retreat indoors within a few minutes, such as a backyard or nearby park — never make your first cold-weather test in remote terrain.
Before heading out, check both the air temperature and wind speed and calculate (or look up) the wind chill, then compare your instinctive sense of how cold it'll feel against the real number.

Dress in your complete planned layering system, then stand still outdoors for about 15 minutes, paying attention to which body parts — fingers, toes, ears, nose — cool first; these are the zones to reinforce with better gear.

Do 10 minutes of easy exertion, such as a brisk walk or carrying a loaded pack, and notice how quickly you begin sweating under your layers — a system that makes you sweat during light activity will chill you dangerously once you stop.
Practice shedding your outer shell layer at the first sign of overheating, and time yourself doing it with gloves on; it should take well under a minute.
If snow is available, spend 15-20 minutes practicing a simple wind block or the start of a snow shelter, timing the effort so you know what it actually costs in a real situation.

With someone else present and water or snow on hand to extinguish it, practice starting a fire using only a ferro rod and tinder or dead-standing wood gathered on site — do this before you ever need it for real.
Set a sealed bottle of water outside in the shade for the duration of the drill and check how much it has cooled by the end, as a concrete illustration of how fast exposed water freezes.
Afterward, debrief with yourself or your group: which gear item did you reach for most, which one underperformed, and what would you change before the next outing.

Only repeat the drill on a colder or windier day once you've comfortably handled a calmer one — cold tolerance and gear confidence should be built incrementally, and any numbness beyond mild tingling is the signal to stop and rewarm immediately.

guides.title: Heat & Desert
guides.summary: Beating heat exhaustion, sun and desert travel.

sections.heading: Travel cool, rest hot
sections.body:
The single decision that most determines whether a person survives a desert on foot is when they choose to move. Air temperature in an arid basin typically peaks two to four hours after solar noon, so the hottest stretch of a summer day is roughly 14:00 to 17:00, not midday. The ground is worse than the air: bare sand, gravel and rock absorb sunlight and re-radiate it, and surface temperatures of 65-80 degrees Celsius (150-175 degrees Fahrenheit) are routinely measured on desert soil while a shaded thermometer at chest height reads 43 degrees Celsius (110 degrees Fahrenheit). Walking through that layer means you are heated from above by direct sun, from the side by air, and from below by a radiating surface at the same time. Travelling instead between about 03:00 and 09:00, and again after sunset, can halve your water requirement for the same distance covered.

The reason a still body needs far less water is arithmetic. Resting metabolism produces roughly 100 watts of heat; walking briskly with a pack produces 400-600 watts. Since evaporating one litre of sweat removes about 2,430 kilojoules (580 kilocalories) of heat, that extra 400 watts of muscular heat alone commits you to roughly six-tenths of a litre of sweat per hour before you account for the heat the sun is adding. A person lying quietly in deep shade in a 43 degree Celsius desert may lose well under half a litre an hour; the same person walking in full sun can exceed a litre and a half. Over a twelve-hour day that difference is the whole contents of a large water bladder.

Sand behaves differently at night too. Dry sand loses heat rapidly after sunset because it radiates efficiently to a clear sky and holds little moisture, and cooler sand is measurably firmer underfoot: the thin films of condensed moisture that form as the surface cools increase the apparent cohesion between grains, so you sink less and waste less energy per step. Desert nights can drop 20-30 degrees Celsius below the daytime peak, and pre-dawn is often near freezing in high deserts such as the Great Basin or the Iranian plateau, so night travel demands an insulating layer you would never carry for the heat alone.

The honest caveat is that night movement carries its own hazards. Navigation error rates rise sharply in the dark, rattlesnakes and other ectotherms are most active in the cooler hours, and a twisted ankle in an unseen wash is far more consequential than heat when you are alone. The workable compromise most desert travellers settle on is to move in the long twilight windows either side of darkness, when there is enough light to read the ground but the sun is below or near the horizon, and to reserve full-dark travel for open, known terrain under a bright moon.

sections.heading: Cover up
sections.body:
Covering up in extreme heat feels wrong and is nevertheless correct, and the reason lies in which heat pathway dominates. Under a desert sun a person receives on the order of 800-1,000 watts per square metre of direct solar radiation, and skin absorbs a large fraction of it. Loose, light-coloured woven cloth reflects and scatters much of that incoming shortwave radiation before it reaches you, while the air trapped in the few millimetres between fabric and skin becomes a slow-moving buffer that still lets water vapour diffuse outward. Sweat evaporates from the skin, migrates through the weave, and evaporates again from the outer surface; you keep the cooling and lose the radiation load. The garment must be loose for this to work. A tight synthetic shirt in contact with skin conducts heat inward and blocks the vapour path, which is why a sweat-plastered t-shirt feels so much worse than a billowing cotton or linen overshirt of the same colour.

The traditional dress of hot-arid cultures encodes this physics. The long robes of the Sahara and Arabian peninsula, the loose cotton of the Indus valley, and the neck-flapped caps of desert armies all solve the same problem: shade the skin, shade the head and neck, and keep air moving underneath. A head covering matters disproportionately because the scalp and the back of the neck sit directly beneath the sun at midday and lie over major blood vessels; the carotid arteries pass within a centimetre or two of the skin surface there. A brim of at least 7-8 centimetres (3 inches) all round, or a cap with a hanging neck flap, does more for perceived heat load than almost any other single item.

Breathing through the nose rather than the mouth is a genuine but modest water saving. The nasal passages act as a counter-current heat and moisture exchanger: incoming air is humidified and warmed by the turbinates, and on exhalation some of that water condenses back onto the cooled mucosa rather than leaving the body. Respiratory water loss in dry desert air runs somewhere around 200-400 millilitres per day at rest and rises steeply with hard breathing, so nose breathing might reclaim a few tens of millilitres an hour. That is not decisive on its own, but it costs nothing, and it has the secondary benefit of keeping the mouth and throat from drying to the point of painful cracking.

Wetting a cloth and draping it over the neck, wrists, groin or inner thighs targets sites where large vessels run close to the surface, so evaporative cooling of the cloth pulls heat out of blood that is about to return to the core. The important caveat is that this only helps if you have water to spare. In a genuine shortage, water on skin is water not in your bloodstream, and drinking it will nearly always do more for your core temperature than wearing it.

sections.heading: Heat illness
sections.body:
Heat illness is a continuum rather than three separate diseases, and knowing where a person sits on it decides whether you rest them or start an emergency. Heat cramps come first: painful involuntary spasms, usually in the calves, thighs or abdominal wall, in someone who has been sweating heavily and drinking mostly plain water. They reflect a sodium deficit in the working muscle rather than simple dehydration, and they resolve with rest, shade, and salted fluid rather than with more water alone. Heat exhaustion is the next stage and the common one: heavy sweating, clammy pale skin, weakness, headache, nausea, dizziness, a fast weak pulse, and core temperature typically between 38 and 40 degrees Celsius (100.4-104 degrees Fahrenheit). Crucially, mental status remains essentially normal in heat exhaustion; the person is miserable and unsteady but coherent, knows where they are, and can follow a conversation.

Heat stroke is a different order of emergency, and the dividing line clinicians actually use is neurological, not thermometric. Any confusion, slurred speech, staggering, bizarre behaviour, combativeness, seizure or loss of consciousness in a hot person is heat stroke until proved otherwise, with a core temperature usually above 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit). At that point proteins begin to denature, the gut lining becomes leaky, an inflammatory cascade resembling sepsis is triggered, and untreated mortality is high. The widely taught rule that heat stroke victims have hot dry skin is unreliable and has cost lives: exertional heat stroke in a young athlete or soldier very often presents with the person still drenched in sweat. Absence of sweating is a late and inconsistent sign, so never use it to rule the diagnosis out.

Treatment priority for suspected heat stroke is cooling before transport, because outcome tracks how long the body spends above roughly 40.5 degrees Celsius. The single most effective field method is cold-water immersion: get the person into a tub, stock trough, creek or any container of cold water up to the neck. Immersion can drop core temperature at around 0.15-0.20 degrees Celsius per minute, far faster than any other practical method, and the target is to cool for roughly fifteen minutes or until they are clearly lucid again. Where immersion is impossible, strip the clothing, drench the skin continuously and fan hard, and pack ice or cold bottles at the neck, armpits and groin. Do not give fluids by mouth to anyone who is confused or has a reduced level of consciousness, because they may aspirate. Summon help at the same time, not afterwards, and keep cooling while you wait, because every minute spent above the threshold matters more to the eventual outcome than the ambulance's arrival time does. Antipyretics such as paracetamol or ibuprofen do nothing for heat stroke and may aggravate the liver and kidney injury that accompanies it, since the raised temperature is not a fever generated by the hypothalamus but a failure to shed heat.

sections.heading: Water & salt
sections.body:
The phrase used by desert soldiers and hydrologists alike is ration your sweat, not your water, and it inverts the instinct almost everyone has when a bottle starts to look low. Human performance degrades measurably at about two per cent body-mass loss from dehydration, which for an eighty kilogram adult is only about 1.6 litres. By four per cent, endurance capacity is cut by roughly a quarter and decision-making is visibly impaired; by six to seven per cent, thermoregulation itself fails because there is no longer enough plasma volume to sustain both skin blood flow and sweat production. Water held in a bottle does nothing for you. Water in your bloodstream is the coolant that keeps you alive, so the correct response to a limited supply is to reduce the rate at which you spend it: move in the cool hours, sit in shade during the heat, drop the pace, and drink when thirsty rather than hoarding.

Salt is the half of the equation people forget. Human sweat contains sodium at roughly 20 to 80 millimoles per litre, which is about 0.5 to 2 grams of sodium chloride per litre depending on genetics, diet and how heat-acclimatised you are. Sweating five litres in a hard desert day can therefore cost 5-10 grams of salt. If you replace those losses with plain water only, blood sodium falls, and the resulting condition, exertional hyponatraemia, produces headache, nausea, confusion and in severe cases seizures from brain swelling. It is genuinely dangerous and it is frequently mistaken for heat exhaustion, which leads bystanders to push still more plain water into the person and make it worse. The practical guard is simple: eat salty food, or add roughly a level quarter to half teaspoon of table salt per litre when sweat losses run high, or use a commercial oral rehydration mix with a real sodium content rather than a sugary sports drink. Note the honest uncertainty here, since sweat sodium varies several-fold between individuals and salt tablets swallowed without adequate water can irritate the stomach and worsen nausea.

The ground deserves separate respect because conduction is a far more efficient heat-transfer path than air. Lying directly on sand or rock that is sitting at 60 degrees Celsius will move heat into your body faster than the same air temperature ever could, and it is a common route to a hot night for anyone who throws down a thin mat in the open. Put something insulating between you and the surface: a closed-cell foam pad, a pack, brush, a folded tarp, anything with trapped air. The same principle works in your favour after dark, when the ground has dumped its heat and now sits well below air temperature; digging fifteen to thirty centimetres into shaded soil often finds material ten degrees cooler than the surface, which is why desert animals burrow and why a shallow scrape in shade makes a genuinely better daytime rest position than sitting on top of the sand.

sections.heading: How the Body Sheds Heat: Thermoregulation Explained
sections.body:
In hot conditions, evaporative cooling from sweat is by far the body's most powerful heat-dumping mechanism: evaporating one litre of sweat carries away roughly 2,430 kilojoules, or 580 kilocalories, of heat, drawn from the latent heat of vaporisation of water. The other three pathways are minor by comparison once air temperature approaches skin temperature. Conduction moves heat into whatever you are touching, convection carries it away in moving air, and radiation exchanges it with surrounding surfaces; but all three depend on a temperature difference between you and your surroundings, and once the air and the sand are hotter than your skin, they run backwards and deliver heat into you instead. Above roughly 35 degrees Celsius ambient, evaporation is essentially the only mechanism left.

Alongside sweating, the body vasodilates, widening blood vessels near the skin to move warm blood from the core to the surface where it can shed heat. This is why skin flushes and pulse rises in heat even before you feel especially hot. Skin blood flow can rise from a baseline of about 0.3 litres per minute to as much as 7-8 litres per minute under severe heat stress, and that redirection has a real cost: cardiac output climbs substantially, heart rate rises perhaps 20-30 beats per minute for the same workload, and blood is diverted away from the gut and working muscle. The competition between skin and muscle for a finite blood volume is precisely why hard work in heat feels disproportionately exhausting, and why cardiovascular strain, not core temperature alone, is often the first thing to give way. A well-acclimatised, fit person doing sustained heavy exertion in heat can sweat 1-2 litres per hour, with a practical ceiling on gut absorption and replacement of around 1-1.5 litres per hour for most people; sustained sweat rates above that simply cannot be matched by drinking, so a deficit accumulates no matter how disciplined the drinking is.

The critical limitation is that evaporation only works when the surrounding air can actually accept more water vapour. Sweat has to evaporate, not merely appear, to cool you; sweat that rolls off the chin and lands in the dirt has cost you the water and bought no cooling at all. The rate is governed by the vapour pressure gradient between wet skin and the surrounding air, which is why high humidity is often more dangerous than high temperature alone. At high relative humidity the air is already close to saturated, sweat beads and drips without evaporating, and the primary cooling system effectively stops even though the person is visibly drenched. This is the physiological reason heat index and wet-bulb temperature describe real risk far better than the number on a dry thermometer, and why 32 degrees Celsius in a humid coastal city can be more lethal than 43 degrees in a dry desert where sweat flashes off the skin almost as fast as it is produced.

sections.heading: Wet-Bulb Temperature: The Real Limit of Human Heat Survival
sections.body:
Wet-bulb temperature is measured with a thermometer whose bulb is wrapped in a wet wick and exposed to airflow. Because evaporation from the wick cools it, the reading is always at or below the actual dry-bulb air temperature, and the gap between the two shrinks as humidity rises. At 100 per cent relative humidity, wet-bulb and dry-bulb temperature are identical, because no further evaporation is possible. That single instrument therefore captures heat and humidity together in one number, which is exactly what a sweating human body cares about. It differs from the heat index used in most American forecasts, an empirical formula fitted to comfort surveys around a baseline humidity that does not correspond to any physical measurement. A useful practical anchor: on a dry desert day at 43 degrees Celsius and 10 per cent humidity, the wet-bulb temperature is only around 22 degrees, while a humid 35 degree Celsius day at 80 per cent humidity gives a wet-bulb near 32 degrees. The desert is far less lethal.

Physiologically, skin temperature under heat stress settles around 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit). Researchers have long cited a wet-bulb temperature of 35 degrees as a theoretical upper survivability limit, because at or above that point there is no vapour pressure gradient between skin and air at all, evaporative cooling stops entirely, and even a resting, unclothed, well-hydrated person sitting in shade with unlimited drinking water will fatally overheat within a few hours purely from their own metabolic heat with nowhere to send it. That threshold is a physical ceiling, not a safety limit.

More recent human-subject work, notably the Pennsylvania State University heat chamber studies, suggests the real-world critical threshold is considerably lower, closer to 30-31 degrees Celsius wet-bulb for young healthy adults doing minimal activity, and lower still for people who are older, unfit, taking medications that impair sweating, or doing any physical work. Wet-bulb readings approaching this range have already been recorded repeatedly in the Persian Gulf, along the Indus valley, and in parts of coastal south-east Asia during extreme heat events, generally for a few hours at a time rather than sustained over days. Climate projections indicate such episodes will become more frequent, longer, and geographically wider, which is the scientific basis behind warnings that some regions may become periodically uninhabitable without mechanical cooling. The practical takeaway for an individual is that in high humidity, shade and rest stop being sufficient protection; only moving air over wet skin, immersion in cooler water, or genuine air conditioning restores a route for heat to leave the body. A fan illustrates both the principle and its limit. Below about 35 degrees Celsius a fan helps considerably, stripping away the saturated boundary layer clinging to your skin. At high humidity, or above roughly 37-40 degrees in dry air, the same fan starts delivering convective heat faster than it removes evaporative heat, which is why public-health guidance in several countries warns against relying on fans alone in extreme heat. Wetting the skin or clothing first restores its usefulness by supplying the water the airflow then evaporates.

sections.heading: Finding and Purifying Water When Stranded in the Desert
sections.body:
If you are genuinely stranded without a reliable water source, the single most important rule is the opposite of instinct: never ration your water intake to make a small supply last longer. Dehydration degrades judgement, coordination and the body's own cooling ability faster than a small water deficit ever saves you, and a person who has carefully preserved two litres while becoming confused and unable to walk has traded away the very capacities that would have got them out. The correct response to a limited supply is to ration exertion, travel only during cooler hours, and seek shade.

To find water, read the landscape rather than searching it at random. Converging animal trails, particularly those of grazing mammals and of bees or doves in the hour after dawn and before dusk, usually funnel toward a drinking point; doves in particular rarely range more than a few kilometres from water. Patches of green vegetation are the strongest single indicator: cottonwood, willow, sycamore, tamarisk and palm are phreatophytes, meaning their roots reach the water table, so a stand of them marks shallow groundwater even where the surface looks bone dry. In a dry wash or arroyo, water sits closest to the surface at the outside of a bend, where the current cut deepest, and at the base of an obstruction such as a rock ledge. Digging a pit half a metre deep at those points, then waiting twenty or thirty minutes for it to seep and for silt to settle, is a far better use of energy than walking to another wash. Slot canyons and shaded rock hollows called tinajas hold rainwater for weeks after a storm because they are shielded from evaporation.

A solar still, a plastic sheet stretched over a pit dug in damp ground and weighted in the centre above a collection container, extracts water by condensing evaporation from the soil. Field tests consistently return well under a litre per day, often only 200-500 millilitres, and the digging itself may cost more sweat than the still returns. Treat it as a supplement in a static camp with shade, not as a strategy. Transpiration bags, clear plastic tied over a leafy living branch, are usually a better return for the effort where vegetation exists, provided the plant is not toxic or milky-sapped.

Any water gathered from a still, seep or pool should be purified before drinking. Bringing it to a rolling boil for one minute kills essentially all bacteria, viruses and protozoa, extended to three minutes above roughly 2,000 metres (6,500 feet) where the lower boiling point gives a smaller thermal margin. Chlorine dioxide tablets are effective but need up to four hours against Cryptosporidium in cold or turbid water, and a filter rated to 0.2 microns removes protozoa and bacteria but not viruses. Purification handles biology only. It does not remove dissolved salts, and stagnant desert pools in alkaline or gypsum-rich basins can be so mineral-laden that drinking them causes osmotic diarrhoea and a net water loss even after perfect treatment. If the water tastes strongly bitter, soapy or salty, and any alternative exists, take the alternative.

sections.heading: Sunburn and UV Overexposure: Recognition and Treatment
sections.body:
Sunburn is direct tissue damage from ultraviolet radiation, mostly UVB in the 280-315 nanometre band, with longer-wavelength UVA penetrating deeper into the dermis and driving long-term ageing and elastin breakdown. UVB photons are energetic enough to be absorbed directly by DNA, fusing adjacent thymine bases into cyclobutane dimers; the visible burn is the inflammatory response as damaged cells are repaired or, where repair fails, deliberately destroyed by programmed cell death. That biology explains the delay everyone underestimates. Peak redness, pain and swelling appear 12 to 24 hours after exposure, long after the sun that caused it, so feeling fine at the time is worthless as a warning signal. The UV Index, published on a scale that commonly runs 0 to 11 and above, is a far better real-time guide than how hot or bright the day feels. UV intensity peaks within a couple of hours either side of solar noon regardless of air temperature, roughly doubles for every 1,000 metres of altitude gained by about 10-12 per cent per thousand metres, and is amplified by reflection: fresh snow bounces up to 80 per cent of incident UV, dry sand about 15-25 per cent, and open water around 10 per cent. Thin or broken cloud blocks little UV while removing the heat that would otherwise warn you, which is why overcast days produce some of the worst burns.

Sunscreen SPF ratings describe UVB blocking only, and the numbers are less linear than they look. SPF 15 filters roughly 93 per cent of UVB, SPF 30 about 97 per cent, and SPF 50 about 98 per cent. The difference between the high numbers is small, and no product blocks everything. What actually determines real-world protection is quantity and reapplication: the laboratory rating assumes 2 milligrams per square centimetre, roughly a full teaspoon for the face and neck and about 30 millilitres for a whole adult body, and most people apply a quarter to half of that, which cuts effective protection disproportionately. Reapply every two hours and immediately after swimming or heavy sweating. Look for the words broad spectrum, which indicate meaningful UVA coverage as well.

For a burn that has already happened, treatment is supportive: cool, not ice-cold, compresses or baths; generous oral fluids, since a large burn shifts fluid into the skin and can dehydrate you; aloe vera gel or a plain moisturiser; and an oral anti-inflammatory such as ibuprofen, which is most effective if taken early, within the first several hours, because it blunts the prostaglandin surge driving the pain. Avoid products containing benzocaine or lidocaine on large areas, as sensitisation reactions are common. Blistering means a second-degree burn: leave blisters intact where possible, cover broken ones with a non-adherent dressing, and watch for spreading redness, pus or fever as signs of infection. Extensive blistering with fever, chills, faintness or vomiting is sun poisoning and warrants medical care. Cumulative lifetime UV dose, and especially blistering sunburns in childhood, is the primary modifiable risk factor for melanoma and other skin cancers, which makes sun protection a long-term health decision rather than a same-day comfort one.

sections.heading: Vehicle Breakdown in the Desert: What Actually to Do
sections.body:
The near-universal advice from search-and-rescue professionals is to stay with your vehicle if it breaks down in remote desert country, unless you know with certainty that help is a short, safe walk away. The reasoning is about detection probability. A car is several square metres of hard-edged, often reflective material that stands out sharply against desert ground in aerial imagery and to the naked eye from a search aircraft; a walking person is a single dot that blends with brush and rock and moves unpredictably away from the last known position. The vehicle also provides shade, a windbreak, a container for supplies, a battery, mirrors, and a fixed point that matches whatever route plan you left with someone. The recurring pattern in fatal desert cases is a person who walked away from a findable vehicle and was located later, sometimes only a few kilometres off, after searchers had already found the car.

Use the shade the vehicle casts rather than its interior. A closed cabin in direct desert sun behaves as a greenhouse and can exceed 60-70 degrees Celsius within an hour, and the metal bodywork itself commonly reaches 60-70 degrees Celsius (140-160 degrees Fahrenheit), hot enough to blister skin on contact. Sit half a metre clear of the panels. The strip of shade migrates around the vehicle through the day, so plan to move with it, and digging a shallow trench beneath that shade reaches subsurface soil that can be several degrees cooler than the surface. Open the doors or windows on the shaded side to vent the cabin if you need to retrieve equipment.

Make the vehicle as conspicuous as you can. Raising the hood is a long-established roadside distress convention and also breaks the vehicle's outline; tie a bright cloth to the antenna, mirror or door handle; lay contrasting material, spare clothing, luggage or branches in a large geometric shape on open ground nearby, since straight lines and right angles do not occur naturally and read instantly from the air. A signal mirror is the single highest-value item you can carry: a well-aimed flash from even a small mirror is visible for many kilometres and has been spotted from aircraft at more than fifty. Aim it by holding two fingers in a V at arm's length, framing the target between them, and walking the reflected bright spot across your own fingers and onto the aircraft. Signals in groups of three, three flashes, three fires, three horn blasts, three whistle blasts, are the internationally recognised distress pattern.

Two persistent myths deserve retiring. Radiator coolant is not an emergency water source: ethylene glycol is sweet-tasting, highly toxic, metabolises to oxalic acid and causes kidney failure, and no amount of dilution or filtering makes it safe. Windscreen washer fluid, typically methanol, is worse. Second, do not idle the engine for air conditioning beyond short deliberate intervals; you will exhaust the fuel and then the battery, and you need that battery for the horn, hazard lights and any chance of a radio or phone charge when a search aircraft or vehicle finally passes.

sections.heading: Heat Acclimatization: Training Your Body Ahead of Time
sections.body:
Heat tolerance is a real, measurable physiological adaptation rather than a matter of willpower or toughness, and it develops on a predictable schedule with repeated heat exposure over roughly seven to fourteen days. The first and largest change is an expansion of blood plasma volume, typically 10 to 12 per cent within the first week, driven by aldosterone-mediated sodium retention and by albumin moving into the vascular space. A larger circulating volume lets the cardiovascular system supply both skin and muscle without the heart having to compensate as hard, which is why resting and exercising heart rates fall by 10-20 beats per minute for identical work after acclimatisation. The second change is in the sweat response itself: sweating starts earlier, at a lower core temperature threshold, so cooling begins before heat has accumulated, and maximum sweat rate rises, in trained individuals from perhaps one litre per hour to two or more. Third, the sweat becomes progressively more dilute as the sweat glands reabsorb sodium more efficiently, with concentrations falling from around 60 millimoles per litre toward 20 or below. That conserves electrolytes across a long day and substantially reduces the risk of cramps and hyponatraemia. Together these adaptations lower both heart rate and core temperature for the same workload, often by a full degree Celsius, compared with an unacclimatised person doing identical work in identical conditions.

The adaptations do not appear at the same rate. Cardiovascular changes and plasma expansion arrive fastest, with most of the benefit present by days four to six; the sweat-gland changes, particularly sodium conservation, take the full one to two weeks and continue improving slowly for several weeks beyond that. Acclimatisation is built through progressively longer periods of heat exposure combined with mild-to-moderate exertion. A standard protocol is 60 to 100 minutes of light-to-moderate activity in the heat, repeated daily, with duration or intensity increased gradually as tolerance builds. Passive exposure such as sitting in a hot room or a sauna produces some plasma-volume benefit but far less of the sweat adaptation, because the stimulus is the combination of elevated core temperature and sustained sweating, not ambient heat alone.

The process is also reversible, and faster than it was gained. Most of the benefit fades within roughly two to three weeks of returning to cool conditions, with plasma volume decaying first, typically losing a noticeable fraction within the first week. This decay explains a well-documented epidemiological pattern: heat illness cases cluster disproportionately in the first genuinely hot days of a season and in the first days after someone travels from a mild climate to a hot one, even when later days that summer are hotter. Anyone planning sustained work in a hot climate, whether a desert crossing, outdoor construction or the start of a summer athletic season, gains measurably from a deliberate one-to-two week ramp rather than starting at full intensity on day one. The honest caveat is that acclimatisation raises the ceiling but does not remove it: an acclimatised person still dies at a sufficiently high wet-bulb temperature, and the improved comfort can tempt people into workloads that remain objectively dangerous.

sections.heading: Desert Heat Myths Worth Unlearning
sections.body:
Several widely repeated pieces of desert survival advice are wrong in ways that get people hurt. Chewing barrel cactus flesh for emergency water is a persistent myth, traceable partly to mid-century adventure films. In reality most barrel cactus pulp is strongly acidic and contains oxalic acid and alkaloids that commonly cause vomiting and diarrhoea; the fluid you might gain is more than offset by the fluid you lose, making it a net negative in exactly the situation where you can least afford one. The narrow exception sometimes cited is the fishhook barrel, Ferocactus wislizeni, and even that is unreliable, varies with the individual plant, and is not something to gamble on. Prickly pear pads and fruit are genuinely edible when the glochids are removed, but they are food with some moisture, not a water source.

Rationing water to make it last is the second dangerous habit. Dehydration degrades the ability to think clearly and to cool yourself well before a modest deficit would have mattered arithmetically, so the correct move is to drink to your body's needs and instead conserve water by cutting exertion and heat exposure. The related myth is that you should sip rather than drink properly; in practice, moderate volumes of 200-300 millilitres at a time are absorbed more effectively than tiny sips, because gastric emptying rate depends partly on stomach volume.

Dark or heavy clothing is often assumed to be simply worse than going shirtless, but the comparison is more nuanced than it appears. Loose, breathable, UPF-rated clothing that covers skin outperforms bare skin in direct sun because it blocks ultraviolet radiation and intercepts solar heating before it reaches you, while still allowing sweat to evaporate through the weave. Colour matters less than people expect: a classic study of Bedouin robes found black and white robes produced nearly identical skin temperatures, because although black absorbs more solar energy at the outer surface, the extra heat drives a stronger convective chimney within the loose garment. The controlling variable is looseness and ventilation, not shade of dye.

Two further beliefs need correcting. The idea that thirst reliably warns you before serious dehydration is unsound: thirst perception lags measurable fluid deficit by roughly one to two per cent body mass, and blunts further with age, which is why scheduled drinking is the standard recommendation for real heat exposure. And the notion that heat stroke victims have hot dry skin has cost lives, because exertional heat stroke frequently presents in someone still visibly sweating; confusion, not dryness, is the diagnostic sign. Finally, alcohol and heavy caffeine before or during heat exposure are worth avoiding, though for different reasons than the folklore suggests: alcohol's diuretic effect is real but modest at ordinary doses, whereas its genuine hazard is impaired judgement about when to stop, and impaired shivering and sweating regulation.

sections.heading: Getting the Gear
sections.body:
Surviving and staying comfortable in serious heat depends on a short list of unglamorous but genuinely effective equipment, and the logic behind each item is worth understanding because substitutions are often possible and improvisation is often necessary. The clothing items exist to intercept solar radiation before it reaches skin while preserving the evaporative path outward, which is why looseness, weave and coverage matter more than fabric fashion; a UPF 50 rating means the material transmits about one fiftieth of incident ultraviolet. The hat's brim dimension is not arbitrary either: a brim shorter than about seven centimetres leaves the ears, nose bridge and neck exposed at the angles where the sun sits during the dangerous hours.

Carrying at least two separate water containers rather than one large one is a redundancy decision. A single punctured bladder or a dropped bottle in a rockfield is a survivable inconvenience with two vessels and a potential emergency with one. Electrolyte products are chosen on sodium content rather than flavour or branding; look for roughly 300-500 milligrams of sodium per 500 millilitres, since most sweetened sports drinks carry far less and function mainly as sugar water. The reflective emergency blanket earns its place twice over, as a shade panel that reflects most incoming radiation when strung above you and as a large, unmistakably artificial signalling surface, at under 60 grams.

Two items are commonly skipped and should not be. The signal mirror is the highest ratio of rescue probability to mass of anything you can carry, and works without batteries, fuel or cell coverage. Purification tablets or a compact filter matter because the water you eventually find in a desert emergency is far more likely to be a stock tank or a stagnant pool than anything clean. Buy these items before you need them and check the sunscreen's expiry date.
ingredients: A wide-brimmed hat (at least a 3-inch brim) or a legionnaire-style cap with a neck flap, from an outdoor/camping retailer or general department store
Loose-fitting, light-colored, tightly woven long-sleeve shirt and pants, ideally with a UPF (UV Protection Factor) rating, from an outdoor retailer
Broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen rated SPF 30 or higher, from any pharmacy or supermarket
Wraparound sunglasses rated to block 99-100% of UVA/UVB, from an optics retailer or pharmacy
An oral rehydration or electrolyte-replacement product (powder, tablets, or pre-mixed) with a meaningful sodium content, from a pharmacy or sporting-goods store
At least two separate water containers or a hydration bladder with a combined multi-liter capacity, from an outdoor/camping retailer
A lightweight reflective emergency (mylar) blanket, which doubles as a rough signaling surface, from an outdoor retailer
A small dedicated signal mirror, or any compact handheld mirror, from a hardware or outdoor store
A bandana, cooling towel, or similar cloth that can be wetted and worn around the neck for evaporative cooling
Water purification tablets or a compact portable filter, from an outdoor/camping retailer
A basic first-aid kit that includes an aloe-vera or burn gel for sunburn, from a pharmacy
A small, non-mercury thermometer to check actual ambient or shade temperature rather than guessing, from a hardware or general retailer

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Running a Heat-Safety Drill
sections.body:
Like cold tolerance, heat safety is a set of skills and personal calibrations best learned on a controlled practice day rather than discovered during a real emergency. The purpose of a drill is not endurance testing; it is to convert vague numbers into personal ones. Sweat rate varies by a factor of three or more between individuals doing identical work, which means published guidance such as drink one litre per hour is at best a starting estimate. Measuring your own body-mass change across a known duration of known effort converts that guesswork into a figure you can plan around, since one kilogram of body-mass loss corresponds almost exactly to one litre of fluid deficit.

Run the drill somewhere with a fast retreat to shade, and treat dizziness, nausea, headache or confusion as an immediate stop signal rather than something to push through. Write the numbers down afterwards; memory of physiological states is unreliable, and a written record is what lets you calculate honest water quantities for a hotter outing months later.
steps: Choose a genuinely hot day (85°F/29°C or above) and run this drill somewhere you can retreat to shade or air conditioning within a couple of minutes, such as a backyard or local park, not remote terrain.
Before heading out, check both the temperature and the humidity or heat index and note them together — this trains you to read combined heat risk rather than just the thermometer.
Fill and note the volume of your water container, then walk at a normal pace in full sun for 20-30 minutes wearing your planned heat-weather clothing.

On returning, note how much water you actually drank versus how depleted you feel, and if practical, weigh yourself before and after in similar clothing to get a rough sense of your personal sweat rate.
Deliberately stand in full sun for two minutes, then move into shade and notice the perceived difference — this calibrates how much shade alone is worth seeking during a real exertion.

Practice basic self-checks for dehydration on yourself now — skin turgor (pinch the back of your hand and see how fast it flattens), urine color, and how you subjectively feel — so you recognize your own baseline before it becomes an emergency read.

Mix an electrolyte drink to the label's recommended concentration and taste-test it in advance, rather than for the first time during an actual heat emergency, so you know whether you'll actually drink enough of it.

If you have access to a car, practice popping the hood, tying a bright cloth to the antenna or mirror, and aiming a handheld mirror to flash reflected sunlight at a distant fixed object, to build real skill at signaling.
Debrief afterward: record how much water you needed for that level of heat and exertion, so you can plan quantities more accurately for longer outings.

Build tolerance and testing intensity gradually — repeat later in the hottest part of the afternoon only once you've handled a milder session comfortably, and treat dizziness, nausea, confusion, or the stopping of sweating as an immediate signal to stop, cool down, and seek help.

guides.title: High Altitude: Thin Air, Altitude Illness & Acclimatization
guides.summary: Above roughly 8,000 feet the air itself becomes the hazard — how to read your body's warning signs, pace an ascent, and know exactly when the only correct move is to go back down.

sections.heading: Altitude Is Its Own Climate, Not Just "Cold and Windy"
sections.body:
Going up a mountain does not merely get colder. The air itself thins in a way that becomes the dominant hazard on its own, entirely independent of temperature, and misreading elevation as simply a colder version of the valley is the most common and most expensive mistake made in this environment. The chemical composition of the atmosphere barely changes with height: oxygen holds at close to 20.9 percent of dry air from sea level all the way past the summit of Everest. What collapses is barometric pressure, and pressure is the force that drives oxygen across the paper-thin membrane of the lung and into the blood. At sea level the atmosphere presses at roughly 760 millimetres of mercury, about 101 kilopascals. By 3,000 metres, near 10,000 feet, it has fallen to about 525 mmHg. By 5,500 metres, near 18,000 feet, it reaches roughly 380 mmHg, almost exactly half of sea level, which means a full breath there delivers about half the oxygen molecules of the same breath taken at the coast. On the summit of Everest at 8,848 metres the pressure sits near 253 mmHg, about a third.

The situation is worse than those raw numbers suggest. Air inside the lung is always fully saturated with water vapour, which exerts a fixed 47 mmHg at body temperature no matter what the altitude is, and exhaled carbon dioxide takes a further share of the remaining space. Because that water-vapour pressure is fixed while the total shrinks, it consumes a steadily larger fraction of the available pressure as you climb, so the oxygen actually reaching the alveoli falls faster than the barometer alone would predict. Nor is a given elevation a fixed pressure: the atmosphere bulges at the equator and thins toward the poles, and a passing low-pressure weather system drops it further still, so the same summit can be physiologically several hundred feet higher on a stormy winter day than on a calm summer one.

Clinically the range is divided into bands. High altitude runs from about 1,500 to 3,500 metres, roughly 5,000 to 11,500 feet, where illness becomes a realistic possibility above about 2,400 metres or 8,000 feet. Very high altitude spans 3,500 to 5,500 metres, where severe illness is common in the unacclimatized. Extreme altitude begins above 5,500 metres, and above roughly 8,000 metres lies the death zone, where no amount of acclimatization is sufficient and the body deteriorates measurably even at complete rest. Layered on top of the thin air come intensified ultraviolet radiation, air so dry it strips fluid with every breath, temperature swings of 20 degrees Celsius or more between noon and midnight, and often genuine cold. Together these make altitude a distinct climate deserving its own preparation, and the fact that it looks like nothing more than a strenuous hike is precisely what makes it dangerous.

sections.heading: How Your Body Responds to Thin Air
sections.body:
The body begins adjusting to reduced oxygen within seconds of arrival and keeps adjusting for weeks, on several overlapping timescales that a traveller can usefully learn to recognize in themselves. The fastest response is the hypoxic ventilatory response: oxygen-sensing cells in the carotid bodies, small clusters of tissue at the fork of the neck arteries, detect the fall in blood oxygen and drive breathing deeper and faster within minutes. Resting heart rate climbs at the same time, often by 10 to 20 beats per minute at 3,000 metres, because moving more blood per minute partly compensates for each litre of it carrying less oxygen. Both responses are useful and both come at a cost, since breathing and pumping are themselves work that consumes oxygen.

Fast breathing has an awkward side effect.
